claims.text: Near-equiatomic alloys containing at least five principal elements have high configurational entropy.
Carbothermal-shock synthesis can produce compositionally uniform high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Carbothermal-shock-synthesized CoCrFeMnNi or similar five-transition-metal nanoparticles are single-phase FCC or BCC with uniform elemental distributions.

The intrinsic thermal stability and diffusion resistance of five-transition-metal HENA depend critically on local lattice distortion and constituent-pair mixing enthalpies rather than on configurational entropy alone.
Insufficient local lattice distortion causes nanoscale phase segregation or grain growth at temperatures significantly below bulk thermodynamic predictions.
Local lattice distortion creates variations in atomic hopping barriers that constitute the primary barrier to diffusion and phase separation.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes homogeneous solid solutions in multi-principal-element alloys.
Sluggish diffusion contributes to thermal stability and reduced grain growth in concentrated solid-solution or high-entropy alloys.
Severe local lattice distortion is the cause of sluggish diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers diffusion activation energies and thereby permits rapid rearrangement and phase segregation.

Traditional alloys are governed primarily by Gibbs-free-energy minimization through intermetallic formation or solubility limits, whereas HENA stability relies on kinetic trapping by lattice distortion.
Large atomic-radius mismatch, including the addition of large-radius elements such as Ta and W, increases local lattice distortion.
A negative heat of mixing produces high local lattice distortion.
High-size-mismatch, negative-mixing-enthalpy nanoparticles will remain single-phase with minimal grain growth up to 1000 K.
Low-size-mismatch nanoparticles with near-zero mixing enthalpy will segregate or amorphize at temperatures as low as 600 K.
The Cantor alloy exhibits sluggish diffusion.
Traditional binary and ternary alloys typically phase-separate at lower temperatures than high-entropy alloys because they have lower mixing entropy.
Below a particle diameter of 3 nm, surface energy dominates over bulk lattice-distortion effects.
Nanoparticle surface diffusion may bypass lattice-distortion-controlled bulk diffusion barriers.
Broadening and shifting of XRD peaks can indicate lattice distortion in high-entropy nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies annealing at 600–900 K, while the conditions specify a broader 600–1200 K range without explaining which range governs the experiment.

The mechanism associates low distortion with similar radii or 'favorable mixing enthalpies,' whereas the prediction associates negative mixing enthalpy, ordinarily a favorable mixing interaction, with high distortion and enhanced stability.

The main hypothesis predicts that negligible distortion makes sluggish diffusion ineffective and leads to instability, but the boundary labels essentially the same high-solubility, negligible-distortion condition as one where the model may fail rather than as a condition predicted by the model.

Retention of stability by one nominally low-distortion alloy would challenge the claimed necessity of distortion, but it would not by itself establish the stronger conclusion that configurational entropy alone caused the stability.
